content.overview: Section 13 sets out the grounds on which either spouse may obtain a decree of divorce, including adultery, cruelty, desertion for not less than two years, conversion, unsoundness of mind, virulent and incurable leprosy (historically), venereal disease in a communicable form, renunciation, and presumption of death, with additional grounds and waiting periods in specified cases.
content.study: Map each ground carefully: cruelty is judged from the petitioner's perspective and need not be physical; desertion requires factum and animus; non-resumption of cohabitation after a restitution or judicial-separation decree can mature into a divorce ground. Distinguish section 13 fault divorce from section 13B mutual-consent divorce. Always check bars under section 23 (taking advantage of one's own wrong, condonation, collusion).

learningObjectives: Explain Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 Section 13 and its statutory purpose.
Identify and apply the provision's ingredients to a factual problem.
Distinguish the provision from related HMA remedies.
enhancement.definition: Section 13 sets out statutory grounds on which a spouse may seek a decree of divorce, subject to the conditions, provisos and procedural safeguards contained in the Act.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A divorce petition must be tied to a specific statutory ground and its ingredients; allegations of marital discord alone are not a substitute for proving a Section 13 ground.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Section 13, read with Section 23 and the applicable provisions governing procedure and relief.
essentialIngredients: Identify the specific Section 13 ground pleaded.
Establish each ingredient of that ground by evidence.
Check statutory periods or conditions where applicable.
Consider Section 23 bars and defences such as condonation, collusion and taking advantage of one's own wrong.
Apply the facts to the selected statutory ground.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 13 contains multiple distinct grounds, so a proper answer must not treat divorce as one generic concept. Cruelty, desertion, conversion, specified mental-health conditions, renunciation, presumed death and other grounds have different elements. The Supreme Court's recent decision in Amutha v. A.R. Subramanian illustrates the need to analyse cruelty and desertion separately under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib). In Amutha v. A.R. Subramanian, judgment dated 19 December 2024, the Court dismissed the wife's appeal and upheld the High Court decree of divorce, treating cruelty, long separation, and irretrievable breakdown as established in that case as sufficient justification; the High Court had found cruelty and desertion under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib).
examples: A spouse alleging cruelty should identify the conduct relied upon, explain why it constitutes mental or physical cruelty on the applicable standard, and then address evidence and any Section 23 bar.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 13 is contested/fault-based statutory divorce; Section 13B is mutual-consent divorce. Section 23 supplies safeguards that can affect relief under Section 13.

caseLaw.name: Amutha v. A.R. Subramanian
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 19 December 2024. The Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the High Court's decree of divorce. It held that cruelty, long separation, and irretrievable breakdown of the marriage, as established in the case, provided sufficient justification for dissolving the marriage. The High Court judgment it upheld had found cruelty and desertion under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib).
caseLaw.relevance: Opened authority on a Section 13 divorce decree upheld by the Supreme Court.

enhancement.problemApplication: Select the pleaded ground, list its statutory ingredients, test the evidence against each ingredient, then examine Section 23 before reaching the result.
examAnswerStructure: Apply the facts and evidence to each ingredient
Conclude with the available statutory relief

Section 13 is contested/fault-based statutory divorce; Section 13B is mutual-consent divorce. Section 23 supplies safeguards that can affect relief under Section 13.
